system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 12 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2155-08-28 05:10:00 to 2155-09-08 20:35:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 1 diabetes, cardiomyopathy (multifactorial, including Chagas disease), and a history of coronary artery bypass grafting was admitted for lightheadedness and bradycardia. He was found to have severe hyperkalemia (K 8.0) with EKG changes including peaked T waves and conduction delays. He received emergency treatment with atropine, insulin, dextrose, calcium, and albuterol, followed by hemodialysis, which normalized his potassium and resolved the arrhythmia. His carvedilol, torsemide, and spironolactone were discontinued due to bradycardia and minimal urine output. He remained stable, with improving electrolytes and no recurrence of symptoms, and was discharged home with plans to follow up with cardiology for pacemaker evaluation and nephrology for dialysis management.
problems: Diabetes with renal manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft

Mr. ___ is a ___ year old man with h/o DM, ESRD on HD MWF, 
pancreatitis, gallstones, who presents with RUQ pain, N/V.

vomiting similar to previous episodes of pancreatitis. In the 
ED, lipase levels were elevated indicative of an acute 
pancreatitis. He was seen by general surgery in the ED who 
determined that the source of the recurrent pancreatitis was 
most likely gallstones versus pancreatic divisum. The patient 
was started on IV fluids, anti-nausea, and pain medications and 
transferred to the floor. Over the course of ___ days, the 
patient's symptoms resolved and he was able to tolerate POs. 
When the symptoms had completely resolved, he was evaluated by 
cardiology, who recommended optimal medical management prior to 
surgery. His blood pressure baseline of 160s-170s was better 
controlled on increased lisinopril and the addition of Imdur. 
When a new SBP baseline of 110s-140s was established, the 
patient was cleared for surgery. 
.
#CCY: The patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy with 
general surgery. Intraoperatively, the patient was found to be 
bradycardic to ___ with a new suspected junctional rhythm 
(elaborated on further below).  The patient was stabilized and 
his heart rate returned to normal, and he was transferred to the 
floor for continued post-operative care. There were no other 
intraoperative complications. On the floor, he was maintained on 
IV fluids in the immediate post-operative period, during which 
time he experienced several bouts of nausea/vomiting x2 days. 
The patient's pain was well-controlled throughout this time. 
When the nausea/vomiting subsided, the patient's diet was 
advanced until he tolerated two full meals (regular diet), after 
which he was deemed stable for discharge.
.
#. HTN: The patient's blood pressure was poorly controlled on 
admission with baseline SBP in 150s-160s. With the addition of 
Imdur 60mg/day and an increased dose of Lisinopril (40mg/day to 
60mg/day), we achieved a new baseline SBP in 110s-140s. The 
patient's blood pressure is always higher on the day of 
hemodialysis, likely secondary to accumulated fluid retention 
over the days between HD sessions. The patient is to continue 
taking Imdur 60mg/day and Simvastatin 40mg/day at home. The 
patient was instructed to take only 40mg/day of Lisinopril 
(admission dose) at home.
.
#. EKG changes: The patient presented initially with ECG 
significant for a new incomplete RBBB pattern and TWI in V1-V3 
compared to priors. Following a bradycardic even 
intraoperatively, his ECG demonstrated diffuse TWI V2-V6 with 
apparent resolution of RBBB pattern. On POD#1, the new TWIs had 
resolved and the RBBB pattern re-appeared. ECG now same as on 
admission. The patient experienced no additional episodes 
related to ECG changes.
.
#. ESRD: The patient continued on hemodialysis per outpatient 
schedule on ___, and ___ throughout the 
admission period without event. Cinacalcet was held per renal 
secondary to hypocalcemia. Continued on other at-home meds, 
including calcium acetate and nephrocaps.

#. DM2: Elevated BG on admission with AG of 17. Gap closed after 
IVF and insulin. At-home insulin doses and sliding scale were 
modified depending on patient's ability to eat. FSBG levels were 
followed throughout his admission without event.

recommendations.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the ___ hospial because you were having 
abdominal pain similar to your previous episodes of 
pancreatitis. We gave you IV fluids and pain medication until 
your symptoms resolved. After 3 days of no eating or drinking, 
you were able to tolerate food/liquids without vomiting and your 
pain/nausea symptoms resolved. You missed your home dose of 
lantus in the morning and thus your blood sugars were high 
tonight. We gave you your lantus this evening and you should 
check your blood sugar before bed and treat it as you would for 
a blood sugar that is elevated prior to bedtime.  Please monitor 
your blood sugars carefully tomorrow and call your doctor if you 
have any questions.  Please take your lantus at lunch time 
tomorrow instead of at breakfast so you do not over dose 
yourself on insulin.

Your recurrent pancreatitis was attributed to gallstones, and so 
you were evaluated by the general surgeons, who recommended 
cholecystectomy (removal of your gall bladder). You were 
evaluated by the cardiologist, who suggested optimizing your 
blood pressure control prior to surgery. As a result, we 
increased your Lisinopril dose to 60mg/day and added Imdur 
(Isosorbide Mononitrate) 60mg/day. With these new medications, 
we achieved better control of your high blood pressure. 
Additionally, your simvastatin was increased to 40mg per day per 
cardiologist recommendations. You should continue taking the 
Imdur 60mg per day and simvastin 40mg per day as an outpatient. 
Please return to taking Lisinopril 40mg (NOT 60mg) per day as an 
outpatient. 

The general surgery team took you to the operating room, where 
you underwent a laparascopic (minimally invasive) 
cholecystectomy (gall bladder removal). During the 
intraoperative period, your heart rate slowed significantly and 
you developed a new cardiac arrhythmia (rhythm disturbance). The 
anesthesiologists were able to bring your heart rate back to 
normal and the new rhythm resolved without further incident. You 
recovered in the post-operative care unit in the immediate 
post-operative period and were transferred back to the internal 
medicine service for long-term recovery. 

While on the floor, you experienced minimal pain and 
nausea/vomiting, for which you were treated with additional pain 
and nausea medication. When your nausea subsided, you were able 
to tolerate fluids by mouth and your diet was advanced 
accordingly. You were discharged home with pain medication.

You received hemodialysis ___, and ___ 
throughout your admission as well as your home medications.

- please start dulcolax 5mg 1 tab daily as needed for 
constipation, hold if loose stool
- No other permanent changes were made to your at-home 
medications, so please continue to take them as they were 
prescribed prior to admission.

than 3 lbs.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  History of pancreatitis and gallstones with acute onset right
upper quadrant pain, nausea, vomiting.

FINDINGS:  Ultrasound of the right upper quadrant demonstrates normal liver
echogenicity and contour.  No focal liver lesions are seen.  Several stones
are seen within the gallbladder fundus.  The gallbladder wall is thickened
measuring up to 7 mm and the gallbladder is moderately dilated.  A small
amount of ascites is seen.  No intrahepatic biliary dilation is seen.  The CBD
is not dilated measuring 3 mm.  The portal vein is patent with hepatopetal
flow.

There are bilateral pleural effusions, right greater than left.  The spleen is
not enlarged measuring 12 cm.  The pancreas is not visualized on this
examination.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Cholelithiasis, gallbladder wall thickening and moderate distention. 
Although cholecystitis is difficult to exclude on these appearances, these
appearances of gallbladder wall in the presence ascites may be due to third
spacing rather than inflammation.
2.  Small amount of ascites.
3.  Bilateral pleural effusions, right greater than left.

base.  There is increased opacification along the lower right chest wall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in last night with severe pain in your upper right abdomen. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I woke up around midnight with sharp pain right here—under my ribs on the right side. I felt nauseous and threw up twice. It felt just like my old pancreatitis episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The ER team ran some tests. Your lipase level was high—518—confirming acute pancreatitis. We also saw gallstones on ultrasound, and your gallbladder wall is thickened. That’s likely what triggered this episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s the gallstones again? I thought I might have something called pancreatic divisum?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible, and we’re considering it. But since you have gallstones and a history of pancreatitis, surgery to remove your gallbladder is the best way to prevent future attacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I’m on dialysis and have heart issues. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. We’ll need clearance from cardiology first. Your blood pressure has been running high—around 160s over 90s—so we’re adjusting your meds to make surgery safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m on lisinopril already. What else are you doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your lisinopril from 40 to 60 mg daily and adding a new medication called isosorbide mononitrate—Imdur—for better blood pressure control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my diabetes? My sugars were high last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 499 with an anion gap of 17. We gave you insulin and fluids. Your gap closed, and your sugars are now stable. We’ll keep monitoring them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my dialysis? I’m usually on MWF.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get dialysis today as scheduled. We held your cinacalcet because your calcium was low, but you’re still taking calcium acetate and nephrocaps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been feeling better since the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and nothing by mouth for now to let your pancreas rest. We’ll recheck labs and see how you’re doing tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Mr. Johnson. Your lipase is coming down, and you’re not vomiting. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still some ache, but not sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll start you on clear liquids today. If you tolerate that, we can advance your diet. Your blood pressure is improving—now in the 130s over 80s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. When will I see cardiology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll see you tomorrow. Once they clear you, we can schedule your cholecystectomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Cardiology reviewed your case. They recommend proceeding with surgery once your blood pressure is stable. We’re close.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How’s my heart? I remember my EKG showed something new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a right bundle branch block, which you’ve had before. There were some T-wave changes, but they’ve resolved. Your heart function remains stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my dialysis yesterday went fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, labs after dialysis look good. Creatinine down, potassium stable. We’ll keep you on the current meds except carvedilol—we lowered the dose to 12.5 mg twice daily to be safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember they stopped it last time I was here for low heart rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re being cautious. Your heart rate is 62 today—normal. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been tolerating a regular diet, and your pain is minimal. Cardiology cleared you for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! When will it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Scheduled for tomorrow morning. We’ll do a laparoscopic cholecystectomy—minimally invasive. Recovery is usually quick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick pre-op check. You’re NPO, right? No food or drink since midnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nothing since 10 PM. I’m a little nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally normal. The anesthesia team is experienced with patients like you. We’ll monitor your heart and blood pressure closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re back on the floor. The surgery went well—your gallbladder was removed laparoscopically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember much after the mask went on. Was everything okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There was a brief moment when your heart rate dropped during surgery, and you developed a temporary rhythm change. The anesthesiologist managed it quickly. Your EKG this morning shows your usual pattern again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in this case. It’s likely due to anesthesia and your underlying heart condition. No damage was detected. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You had some nausea yesterday. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Only threw up once. Can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids. If you keep that down, we’ll advance to solid food. Pain under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the acetaminophen helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full meals and no vomiting. That’s great progress. We also did a chest X-ray before surgery—shows a slightly enlarged heart and a small right pleural effusion, but nothing new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my heart condition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes. But no signs of congestion. You’re doing well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final day! You’ve tolerated a regular diet, your incision looks good, and labs are stable. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue most as before. We’re adding Imdur 60 mg daily and increasing simvastatin to 40 mg. But go back to your original lisinopril dose—40 mg, not 60.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the dulcolax?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take one tablet daily if you’re constipated. Stop if you have loose stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had dialysis yesterday and did well. We’re just waiting on your last set of vitals before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’ll go home today. Take oxycodone only if needed for pain, and only for two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a follow-up with surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in one week. Also, continue with nephrology and cardiology as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And weigh myself daily?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call if you gain more than three pounds in a day. Otherwise, you’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re being discharged home with services. Someone will help with your dialysis access care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my daughter will help until I’m fully recovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And remember—check your blood sugar regularly. You missed your Lantus this morning, so we gave it last night. Take it at lunch tomorrow to avoid overdose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll set a reminder. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. We’ll have your discharge papers ready shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your gallbladder pathology report isn’t back yet, but it’s not urgent. We’ll send it to your primary care doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, no problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your transplant status is still active. Nephrology will keep you updated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hopeful. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, follow the instructions, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse says your ride is here. Ready to go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m ready. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in—how are you feeling at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, doctor. Ate breakfast, no nausea. Blood sugar was 140.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep it up. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your dialysis is scheduled for tomorrow. Any questions before I sign off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, all clear. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update—your post-op vitals from home nurse are stable. Keep following the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Feeling stronger every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check-in. You’ve been discharged, and all is well. We’ll close this admission now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate all your care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease, type 2 diabetes, cardiomyopathy due to Chagas disease, and a history of coronary artery bypass grafting was admitted for acute gallstone pancreatitis. He presented with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting, and was found to have elevated lipase and gallstones on ultrasound. He was managed conservatively with IV fluids and pain control while optimizing his blood pressure with increased lisinopril and addition of isosorbide mononitrate for surgical clearance. He underwent a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, during which he experienced transient bradycardia and a temporary junctional rhythm that resolved without intervention. Postoperatively, he had mild nausea but tolerated a regular diet and recovered well. His medications were adjusted, including continuation of Imdur and increased simvastatin, while reverting to his prior lisinopril dose. He received hemodialysis as scheduled and was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up plans.
